task_row_model.query: In C++, how can I implement a thread-safe LRU cache that provides O(1) get and put operations while minimizing contention under high concurrency? Describe a practical design and trade-offs for production use.

documents.content: A conventional LRU cache uses a hash table mapping keys to nodes and a doubly linked list to maintain recency. On a single thread both get and put are O(1): lookup the map, move the node to the head of the list, and evict from the tail when capacity is exceeded. For concurrency one simple approach is to protect both the map and list with a single mutex or a read/write lock: readers use shared access and writers upgrade to exclusive, but a global lock serializes updates and can become a bottleneck under heavy parallel writes.

An LFU (least-frequently-used) cache counts the number of accesses per key and evicts the least used when full. Typical designs maintain frequency buckets and a map from key to a node in a frequency list. LFU gives better retention for hot items in workloads with skewed access patterns, but maintaining exact frequency under concurrency requires careful atomic counters or locks per bucket, and the update complexity can be higher than LRU. LFU is a different eviction policy and does not address LRU-specific concurrency techniques.

If unordered_map rehashing causes latency spikes, pre-sizing and reserving buckets reduces rehash cost: call reserve(capacity) during initialization and choose a load_factor consistent with desired memory use. Also consider using custom hash functions for the key type to avoid clustering. For throughput, avoid expensive key-copying by storing movable types or pointers. These measures improve map performance and allocation behavior but do not by themselves provide thread-safety or LRU semantics under concurrency; you still need synchronization around the map and list structures.

A practical high-concurrency design shards the cache into N independent segments, each a small LRU (unordered_map + doubly linked list) protected by its own mutex. Hash the key to pick a shard so get/put only lock that shard, achieving O(1) ops per shard and greatly reducing contention. Use std::shared_mutex if reads dominate, allowing concurrent lookups without blocking each other, but write operations still take exclusive locks. Maintain per-shard size and evict in-shard when its capacity is exceeded; global capacity is approximate (sum of shard capacities). Trade-offs: complexity, uneven load across shards, and higher memory overhead versus a single global LRU.

Lock-free or wait-free LRU implementations are challenging because the LRU list is inherently mutable. Some systems use an approximate LRU: store a timestamp or access counter in a concurrent hash map and run a background thread that periodically scans and evicts the oldest entries. Another approach is to combine a concurrent hash map (e.g., per-bucket locks) with a best-effort recency queue where moving nodes is relaxed: on access mark the node and append to a log; a background compactor rebuilds recency. These reduce contention but sacrifice strict LRU guarantees and require careful memory reclamation.
